title: About
text:
I grew up in New Plymouth, a small town in southwestern Idaho, where the public schools were one of the places the whole community came together. Most of what I study today traces back to that experience: who governs our schools, who gets a voice in those decisions, and what schools teach us about being citizens.
I studied political economy at The College of Idaho, then earned an M.A. in political science at Duke University and a Ph.D. in Politics & Education at Columbia University. At Teachers College, I learned to treat education as a political institution, not only a policy area, and taught graduate seminars on American politics and education, federalism, and the policy process. Being hooded by Jeffrey Henig at commencement remains one of my favorite memories.
After Columbia, I was a postdoctoral researcher at Brown University with the Annenberg Institute and the Realizing Rights Lab. There I ran exit polls in school board elections alongside undergraduate students, and deepened my work on administrative burden and access to democratic participation.
Today, I am an Assistant Professor of Political Science at North Central College, where my office sits in Goldspohn Hall. I live in Chicago and make the commute out to Naperville, which gives me time to think (and to listen to more Taylor Swift than I would care to admit). I still follow Idaho education policy closely, and I write about it for Idaho Ed News whenever I can.
Outside of work, you can usually find me watching the latest Netflix show, catching up on pop culture, or exploring a new corner of Chicago.

title: I study how schools shape democracy, and how democracy shapes schools.
text:
Political Science · Education Politics



I am an Assistant Professor of Political Science at North Central College, where I teach American politics, political behavior, public policy, and education politics. I am also a research affiliate at Brown University’s Annenberg Institute and the Realizing Rights Lab.
I study the politics of K–12 education because public schools are among the last places where Americans of different backgrounds can still govern something together. My work explores when that works, when it doesn’t, and what it means for democracy.

title: I study how schools shape democracy, and how democracy shapes schools.
text:
Research areas


Partisanship & school boards
How national partisanship reaches local school board elections, from exit polls in school board races to a national measure of district partisanship.


Administrative ease & access
How the design of public institutions makes participation easier or harder, from the costs of voting in elections to accessing special education information via school districts.


Education federalism
How authority over schooling is divided across levels of government, including state spending priorities and the dissolution of the U.S. Department of Education.

title: Research
text:
My research examines how educational institutions shape democratic participation and how citizens shape the governance of public education. I focus on the politics of education governance, administrative ease in democratic participation, and the role of schools in producing civic engagement.
Across projects, I combine original data, such as school board election exit polls and web-scraped district information, with large administrative datasets to understand how institutional design shapes citizens’ access to democratic participation.
